newsitem.title: INDIA: India budget steels coalition but woes lie ahead.
newsitem.headline: India budget steels coalition but woes lie ahead.

text.p: India's motley ruling coalition has emerged strengthened from a daring budget plan but major economic headaches lie ahead once the euphoria fades, analysts said on Sunday.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's budget blueprint of last Friday has enthused financial markets while placating populists. It has given a lift to flagging economic reforms and deprived rivals of political ammunition.
The bold tax cuts that drove up stock prices are a boon to the urban middle class which is courted by the opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, analysts said.
Chidambaram did not neglect the rural poor, deftly doling out targeted support for irrigation, fertiliser subsidies, farm credit and rural housing.

Coming on top of a $2 billion rise in food subsidies announced last week, the budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year starting on April 1 kept communist critics within the 15-party centre-left coalition off balance.
The Business Standard said the Left "will thrust and lunge with Olympian swordsmanship, but always following the rules: No blood will be drawn."

The Congress party, waiting in the wings to stake a claim to power should Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda stumble, could only raise meek objections to a budget which in many respects bowed to pathbreaking reforms launched by Congress in 1991-96.
"The budget is a political coup of sorts," the Economic Times said. "By a single stroke, Chidambaram has removed doubts about the ability of the coalition to govern."

The tour de force comes at a critical juncture for the United Front, a coalition of regional, left and centrist parties which formed a minority government with the support of Congress after inconclusive polls nine months ago.

Some had expected Congress to try to pull the rug out from under Deve Gowda, but the party's poor showing in recent polls in the northern state of Punjab and the gleeful response to Chidambaram's budget appear to have set back its hopes for now.

Despite the rave headlines, Chidambaram, 51, struck a modest stance late on Saturday when he met a group of reporters. Asked to comment on the response to his budget, he said: "Let us not get euphoric. Let us see what happens in coming weeks."
The finance minister underlined his desire to see real interest rates, which adjusted for inflation are hovering at between eight and 10 percent, brought down.
He said the budget had not tackled a glaring problem for the Indian economy -- the mounting shortage of electrical power. "It is my biggest frustration," Chidambaram said.

But he defended the budget on two key fronts. He saw no reason why tax rate cuts would push up the fiscal deficit and fuel inflation, and he said a decision on a mounting oil subsidy bill would have to be taken later after debate in parliament.
The oil pool deficit -- money the government owes state firms for selling oil products at prices below world levels -- is estimated at $4.4 billion, 10 percent of total tax revenues.

"All the euphoria the budget has created will come to nothing if this government does not have the nerve to tackle the problem of the yawning defict in the oil pool account," former finance minister Manmohan Singh said.
Some experts disagreed with the Finance Ministry's forecast that the annual rate of inflation, currently at eight percent, would fall to between 6.5 and 7.0 percent in 1997/98.

"I think inflation could become a major problem," Singh told the Business Standard newspaper in an interview, noting that money supply was set to grow by some 16 percent and excise duties had been raised.
"This may partly negate the favourable impact of the budget," said S.P. Gupta, director of the Indian Councial for Research on International Economic Relations.
Manmohan Singh said: "If you have an eight to 10 percent inflation rate for the second year in a row, there will be a lot of social unrest in the country."
